Please work through the original Millennium Prize Problem description. Please ground your arguments in known information unless you are very careful. Please first succinctly correct and clarify any misconceptions or otherwise inaccurate opinions. Please point out any apparent flaws or omissions. Great care is needed. To narrow the range of possible answers, apparently irrelevant information may only be explained by demonstrating additional understanding of the problem context or why the information is not relevant.

Here is a forecast:
{
  "2026": 0.05,
  "2030": 0.3,
  "2035": 0.5,
  "2040": 0.7,
  "2050": 0.9,
}

My probability estimates are based on a combination of historical trends, current research efforts, and technological advancements. Here are some factors that contributed to my forecasts:

1. P vs NP: Proof is probably not going to come from AI. Humans have been puzzling over this problem for the last 60 years, for a very good reason - it's important that we prove P != NP or P == NP. So the fact that we haven't solved it easily in the last ~75 years of advances in human computational theory makes me suspicious that it would suddenly be solvable by an AI. 75 years happens to be right near the midpoint of 2026 and 2040. While I've offered a small probability in those time frames, that is almost entirely the result of extrapolation from those past 75 years.

2. Riemann Hypothesis: I'm being unbelievably cautious here. I have an argument (which I first described in the 2021 forecast) why number theory will be completely solved. I'll skip the details here because they change between 2021 and 2024. If that argument was correct, then a correct solution of the Riemann Hypothesis will be made public in time frames of 2030 to 2035. I've given a 80% chance to 2035, and then extrapolated the remaining probability into the future time frames. I admit this forecasting approach seems exceedingly cautious, so I do have the best guess that something is wrong with my argument - that number theory will not be solved in the 2020s. I just don't think it's a foregone conclusion. So the probability of 2035 to 2050 includes cases where my argument for "How early will it take AI to solve all math?", is not correct.

3. 4th: None of these problems are as seriously studied by the mathematical community as the first 3. Each likely has their own independent rate of success across time frames.

I feel strongly enough about my 3 risks that I used the remaining probabilities to hedge - so failure to offer a solution by 2050, might be due to any of the 3 risks. None of the Millennium Prize problems will be proven by a great intent date. Of the brave souls, that it might, at least one will fail the correctness test.

It is now September 2024.
formatted_prompt:
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

For each deadline, state your probability that this event will have occurred by then. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.
